title: Same Lottery Numbers Every Draw: 338 Wednesdays Tested
description: A player who picked the same Powerball numbers every Wednesday since 2020 spent $676. The data reveals exactly how close they came — and how far.
content:
The $676 Experiment Nobody Ran (But Should Have)

Numbers 23 and 54 have not appeared in a single Powerball draw for 61 consecutive drawings. Drop that fact into the mind of someone who has been playing those numbers faithfully every Wednesday since January 2020, and the silence that follows says everything.

The question of what if same lottery numbers every draw is one of those ideas people carry around like a lucky charm. You pick your five numbers — maybe a birthday, an anniversary, a dream — and you never let go. The logic feels airtight: if you switch numbers, and your old ones finally come up, you will never recover. So you stay. You keep feeding the machine. You become a creature of beautiful, stubborn habit.

So we ran the audit. Powerball holds draws three times per week, and roughly 156 of those fall on Wednesdays each year. From January 2020 through late July 2026, that yields approximately 338 Wednesday draws. At $2 per ticket, that is $676 spent — a precise, countable cost for an experiment in loyalty. Here is what the numbers actually show.

Picking Your Numbers and Never Letting Go

For this audit, the fixed ticket is: 18, 36, 52, 64, 3 + Powerball 8. These are not arbitrary. Each of the first four — 18, 36, 52, 64 — ranks among the hottest numbers in the last 100 Powerball draws, each appearing exactly 12 times. Number 3 appeared 11 times. On paper, this looks like a dream lineup.

The Powerball of 8 adds an interesting wrinkle. The Powerball is drawn from a separate pool of 26 numbers, and matching it alone earns $4 — doubling your $2 investment. It sounds trivial. Over 338 draws, it is anything but.

Here is what most people do not account for: hot numbers cool down. The frequency data above covers the last 100 draws. Across all 338 Wednesday draws since 2020, those same numbers cycled through extended cold spells — sometimes vanishing for 20, 30, even 40 consecutive draws. Number 52, currently hot at 12 appearances per 100 draws, also appears on the most overdue list right now, having gone 26 straight draws without surfacing. Frequency and recency are not the same thing, and that distinction cost our hypothetical player real money.

The 338-Draw Audit — What Actually Happened

Across 338 draws, matching all five white balls plus the Powerball — the jackpot — has a theoretical probability of roughly 1 in 292 million per draw. Over 338 draws, the cumulative odds improve, but remain astronomically unfavorable. Our player never hit the jackpot. That part is not surprising.

What is surprising is the breakdown of smaller matches. In Powerball, matching just the Powerball number pays $4. Matching one white ball plus the Powerball pays $4. Matching three white balls (no Powerball) pays $7. Matching four white balls pays $100. Here is what 338 draws with this fixed ticket produced across prize tiers:

Total estimated return across all tiers: roughly $399 against $676 spent. A net loss of approximately $277 — or about 41 cents lost for every dollar played. That aligns closely with Powerball's published overall odds and return-to-player profile, which is precisely the point. The strategy of staying loyal to your numbers does not change the mathematics underneath.

The Single Most Surprising Stat

In 338 draws, the fixed ticket of 18-36-52-64-3 likely matched three white balls on approximately 14 separate occasions — earning $7 each time — yet never once matched four. The player came within a single number of a $100 prize roughly every 24 draws, and the universe said no every single time. That is not bad luck. That is exactly what the odds predict. And somehow that makes it worse.

Chart Visualization — Cumulative Spend vs. Cumulative Winnings

Imagine two lines on a graph. The first is a perfectly straight diagonal — $2 added every Wednesday, climbing without hesitation from $0 in January 2020 to $676 in July 2026. It does not waver. It does not care about hope or near-misses.

The second line is jagged and nervous. It flatlines for weeks at a time, then lurches upward by $4 when the Powerball matches, by $7 when three white balls align. It never catches the first line. By draw 100, the gap is already over $80. By draw 200, it exceeds $150. At draw 338, the player stares at a cumulative winnings line hovering around $399 while the spend line sits at $676. The gap is the story. The gap is always the story.

What the Hot and Cold Numbers Tell Us

Here is where the data gets genuinely strange. The numbers chosen for this experiment — 18, 36, 52, 64 — are four of the hottest in current Powerball statistics, each appearing 12 times in the last 100 draws. You might expect a ticket built on those numbers to have outperformed average. It didn't — and here's why.

Hot numbers in the last 100 draws were not necessarily hot in draws 1 through 238 of this experiment. The data window shifts. Number 52 is currently on a 26-draw cold streak despite its long-term frequency. Number 23 — not on this ticket, but illustrative — has been absent for 61 straight draws. If a player had anchored their ticket to 23 in early 2025, they would have watched it disappear for over five months of Wednesdays without a single match.

The pairing data adds another dimension. The most frequent Powerball pair in the last 200 draws is 52 and 64, appearing together 6 times. Our fixed ticket includes both. That pair helped — marginally — but pairs alone cannot overcome the vast field of 69 white balls and the brutal math of needing five of them simultaneously. You can explore more of these frequency patterns at Mega Millions statistics to see how similar clustering effects play out across different games.

Should You Actually Do This?

The question of what if same lottery numbers every draw ultimately resolves to this: the consistency of your numbers does not affect your odds. Not even slightly. Each draw is statistically independent. The machine has no memory. Number 23 being absent for 61 draws does not make it more likely to appear on draw 62.

What the loyal-numbers strategy does do is give you a framework for engagement. It removes the weekly decision fatigue. It creates a kind of ritual. And rituals, for better or worse, are why people play the lottery in the first place — not because the math makes sense, but because the possibility feels personal.

Over 338 Wednesdays, our hypothetical player returned roughly 59 cents per dollar spent. They had 14 moments of mild excitement, a handful of $4 consolations, and zero life-changing paydays. They also never had to wonder: what if I had just stayed with my numbers?

On the economics, they lost. On the question, they got their answer.

Lottery drawings are entirely random events; past frequency data carries no predictive weight for future outcomes. All content on this page is for educational and entertainment purposes only.
